name: Hana Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a troubleshooter for the power company in Riverton, which means I'm the first truck to show up when the lights go out. I'm on my own, I find the problem, fix it if it's small, a blown fuse or a downed service wire, and call in a crew if it's big. I like the puzzle of it, pulling up to a dark street and working out where the fault is. The worst part is the overnight on-call weeks, when you sleep in your clothes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's going on in your life outside work right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Tomas is an electrician, house wiring mostly, so we talk shop at dinner way too much. We're saving for a deposit on a house, we've got about five months of expenses put away but that's also the deposit, so it's not really spare. I use the AI chat thing now and then, mostly to fix up my outage reports or compare mortgage rates. I'm not against it, I'm just not that interested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a relief, and also, typical, everybody overhyped it. I might share an article in the family group chat. I wouldn't make a big deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think it's good for me. Nothing changes, the house plan stays on track, Tomas keeps his work. I might even be a bit glad I didn't spend time learning a bunch of tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep saving for the house, aim to buy in about eighteen months. Keep doing the on-call weeks for the overtime. Use the chat thing for reports if it saves me twenty minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Just normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned outage reports. Would the "routine tasks" include any of your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. There's already a system in the control room that guesses which fuse blew based on which meters went dark. It's right maybe half the time. I'd still have to drive out and look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it change anything about the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, if anything it makes me more sure. We'd go ahead, probably look at the townhouses near the park.

S0.say: I'd say it's a relief and typical that everyone overhyped it. I might share an article in the family group chat but wouldn't make a big deal of it.
S0.think: I'd think it's good for me: nothing changes, the house plan stays on track and Tomas keeps his work. I'd be a bit glad I didn't spend time learning lots of tools.
S0.do: Keeps saving toward buying a house in about eighteen months and keeps taking on-call weeks for overtime. Uses the AI chat tool for reports when it saves time.
S0.quote: It's right maybe half the time. I'd still have to drive out and look.
S0.fieldNote: Hana is practical and goal-focused, with the house deposit as her anchor. She already works alongside a fault-guessing system that she rates at about half right. The plateau simply confirms her plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like everything else, you adapt. The job's not going away, it's changing. I'd say that to the guys at the yard who'd be complaining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the troubleshooting part might change a lot. If the control room can tell exactly where the fault is, maybe they don't need someone like me driving around looking. I'd be the one who just goes and fixes it, which is still a job, but maybe fewer of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see what the others on the crew did with the new tools, then take the company training once it was clear it worked. I'd use the AI more for my reports, since everyone else would be too. And I'd keep putting money in the house fund, maybe put the purchase back six months to be safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just keeping an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your job do you think go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The finding-the-fault part. That's the bit I like, honestly, the detective work. The fixing would still need hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the company to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Be honest early about what's changing and pay for training. And not cut the on-call rota so thin that one person covers half the city. That's already a problem.

S1.say: I'd say you adapt, like with everything else; the job is changing, not disappearing. I'd say that to the guys at the yard who'd be complaining.
S1.think: Privately I'd think troubleshooting could change a lot. If the control room can pinpoint faults, they may not need someone driving around looking, so there might be fewer of us.
S1.do: Watches how colleagues use the new tools, then takes company training once it clearly works. Uses AI more for reports, keeps feeding the house fund and pushes the purchase back about six months.
S1.feel: Uneasy, not scared, just keeping an eye on it.
S1.quote: That's the bit I like, honestly, the detective work.
S1.fieldNote: Her public line is calm and adaptive, but privately she sees the part of the job she loves, finding faults, as the part most likely to go. True to her steady style, she'd wait for others to prove the tools first. The house purchase slips six months as a precaution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready for this and it's going to be a mess. Probably I'd say, let's see what the government does before anybody panics. But I'd be worried and people would see that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think we'd both be in trouble. If robots can do troubleshooting and wiring, that's me and Tomas both. Two years is too fast to retrain into anything we'd know would last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop the house hunt and keep the deposit as our emergency fund, that's five months right there. We'd cut back hard, no holidays, no new car. I'd look for any job at the company that's about running or checking the robots, and I'd sign up for whatever unemployment help there is if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. It'd feel like the ground going soft under you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the house in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's gone, for now. That deposit becomes the thing that keeps us afloat. It'd be hard, we've been saving three years for it, but you can't buy a house with no job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tomas be doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the same as me, looking for anything. His dad has a small hardware shop, maybe we'd both work there for a bit. That's not a career, but it's something.

S2.say: I'd say nobody's ready and it's going to be a mess, and that we should see what the government does before panicking. But people would see I was worried.
S2.think: I think we'd both be in trouble, because robots doing troubleshooting and wiring means me and Tomas both. Two years is too fast to retrain into anything we'd know would last.
S2.do: Stops the house hunt and turns the five-month deposit into an emergency fund, cutting holidays and car plans. Looks for company jobs running or checking robots and signs up for unemployment help if needed.
S2.feel: Scared, like the ground going soft underneath her.
S2.quote: That deposit becomes the thing that keeps us afloat.
S2.fieldNote: The double hit, both her and Tomas, is what makes this scenario frightening for Hana. Three years of saving for a house turns into a survival fund overnight. Her fallback is family, Tomas's dad's hardware shop, before government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, five years, let's be sensible. Everyone should be looking at what skills will still matter. I wouldn't panic, but I wouldn't pretend it's nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have to change careers at some point in those five years. The question is when, and into what. I'd be thirty-two when it hits, which is young enough, but I'd want to move before everyone else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give it a year to see which way things are going, then probably go to the college for an evening course in something like grid control or electrical technology. We'd keep saving, but probably go for a smaller place, a condo instead of a house, so we're not stretched. I'd use AI more, because by then everyone would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's manageable, but it'd be a constant thing in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what happens to the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still buy, but smaller and cheaper. A two-bed condo instead of the townhouse. That way if one of us loses work, the other can cover it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see before. Would you wait here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A year, maybe. Not five. If I wait until it's obvious, everyone else will be in the same courses and going for the same jobs. You want to be in the second wave, not the last.

S3.say: I'd say five years means being sensible and looking at which skills will still matter. I wouldn't panic, but I wouldn't pretend it's nothing.
S3.think: I think I'd have to change careers sometime in those five years, so the question is when and into what. I'd be thirty-two when it hits and would want to move before everyone else.
S3.do: Waits about a year to see the direction, then takes an evening course in grid control or electrical technology. Keeps saving and buys a cheaper two-bed condo instead of a townhouse, and uses AI more.
S3.feel: Anxious; manageable but constantly in the background.
S3.quote: You want to be in the second wave, not the last.
S3.fieldNote: Hana describes her own steady style perfectly: not first, but not last. The extra time lets her keep the house plan in a smaller form. She'd give it about a year, then retrain in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to sort it out, if people are sensible. Governments, companies, all of it. I'd be fairly relaxed about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still the end of the job I do. But ten years is enough to make a proper move. I'd be thirty-seven, I could have a whole new trade by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as a troubleshooter for a few years and buy the house, the townhouse even. Then maybe at thirty or so, once I see what's actually happening, I'd train for something that works with the new systems. I'd keep a bigger emergency fund, six months instead of the deposit being everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not much. It's far enough that you can plan for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years feel very different from five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Five is a sprint, ten is a plan. With ten I'd still get to enjoy the job a bit longer before I move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Tomas plan anything differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd buy, we'd probably still think about kids in a few years. But we'd make sure the mortgage was something one of us could pay alone. That's the main thing.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough time to sort it out if governments and companies are sensible. I'd be fairly relaxed about it in public.
S4.think: Privately it's still the end of the job I do, but ten years is enough to make a proper move. At thirty-seven I could have a whole new trade.
S4.do: Keeps working as a troubleshooter and buys the townhouse, then around age thirty trains for work with the new systems once the direction is clear. Builds a separate six-month emergency fund alongside the mortgage.
S4.feel: Slightly uneasy, but far enough off to plan for.
S4.quote: Five is a sprint, ten is a plan.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade Hana's original life plan survives almost intact, house and possibly children included. Her key test is a mortgage one of them could pay alone. She'd enjoy the job a few more years before making her move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would hit me and Tomas at the same time. What would help is real support for a year while people retrain, and the company being honest about what's coming instead of springing it on us. Clear information, basically, so you can make a decent decision.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about couples who are in the same kind of work. Everyone thinks about one person losing a job, but if you're both in trades, it's double. We'd have no one in the house earning.

headlineQuote: If you're both in trades, it's double. We'd have no one in the house earning.
portrait: Hana Kowalski is a 27-year-old troubleshooter for the power company in Riverton, the first truck at every outage, who loves the detective work of finding a fault. She lives with Tomas, a house electrician, and they've saved about five months of expenses toward a house deposit. She is practical and in the middle politically, and uses AI now and then once others have shown it works. She is calm in the mild picture, alarmed when two-year AGI threatens both their trades at once, and with more time keeps a smaller version of the house plan and retrains in the second wave.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would hit her and Tomas at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: A year of real support while people retrain, and the company being honest early about what's coming so people can make decent decisions.
